title: Great Leaders Dont Just Select Talent, They Ensemble It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article distinguishes between two leadership talents: picking individually strong performers and, the rarer skill, assembling those individuals into a team whose members complement and elevate one another. It describes leaders who think in terms of chemistry, fit, and contrast rather than a checklist of star qualities, deliberately mixing generations, styles, and backgrounds so people push each other to grow. The piece frames team construction as an ongoing, adjustable recipe rather than a one-time hiring decision, and closes by asserting that assembling complementary talent matters even more than finding great talent individually.
points: Selecting individual talent and ensembling a team are two distinct, both valuable, leadership skills.
Great ensemblers prioritize chemistry and complementary fit over a checklist of star qualities.
Mixing generations, styles, and levels of experience is a deliberate tactic, not an accident.
Team composition is treated as an evolving recipe that leaders keep adjusting.
quotes: But there’s another talent judgment that is equally important and perhaps even more rare—the ability to ensemble talent.
Leaders great at ensembling talent think first about the chemistry and fit between individual talents and skills.
But most of all, they want individuals who will push the buttons that others on the team need to be pushed.
They know it is the unexpected chemistry between qualities (think peanut butter and chocolate) that can make all the difference.
An ensemble of the right stars makes the night sky of any team brighter. Great leaders know how talent fits together.
